title: Tenant Fencing & Prefetch Strategy Architecture Review
summary: Deep technical review covering multi-tenant fencing, KV prefetch+eviction strategies, batching/latency tradeoffs, quantization impacts, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Customer wants deterministic throughput for peak 99th percentile latency and an approach for guaranteed capacity with graceful fallbacks.
topics: multi-tenant isolation and noisy neighbor mitigation
KV cache prefetch and eviction policies
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-05 15:00 UTC | Duration: 57 mins | Recording: enabled
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Aisha Rahman (CTO, NovaPay), Tom Burke (Platform), Sara Vega (Security), Jin Park (SRE)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Okay everyone thanks for carving out the time today. The goal is to walk through tenant fencing, prefetching ideas for the KV cache, and how we think about dedicated vs hosted fallback guarantees. We'll flag tradeoffs on latency and cost.
[00:18] Aisha Rahman: Thanks Maya. Just to set context, we're a payments platform, peak spikes around end of month, and we're very sensitive to 99th percentile latency. We also have strict PCI-ish controls, so VPC or on-prem are on the table depending on the audit.
[00:32] Liam O'Connor: Got it. We'll call out the options: fully dedicated pools, hybrid pinned shards, and multi-tenant with fencing controls and QoS. Quick question on peak throughput numbers if you have them.
[00:45] Tom Burke: For the busiest flows it's roughly 600 qps with bursts to 1.4k qps for short windows, median token length about 80, but some sessions go to 600 tokens for long receipts.
[00:58] Priya Patel: Thanks. That's helpful — that token distribution really shapes batching and KV cache sizing.
[01:10] Aisha: Also the security ask — we need KMS integration, audit logs for prompts and responses (redaction ok), and SSO/SAML for console.
[01:22] Sara Vega: And retention controls: we want customer prompt logs to be purged after 90 days unless flagged.
[01:30] Maya: Totally. We'll include SOC2 docs and the KMS integration flow; we'll note retention config in the pilot runbook.

[01:40] -------------------- Technical details --------------------
[01:42] Liam: Starting with tenancy: dedicated pools are simplest for guarantees — fenced GPUs, full cache warm per tenant, predictable throughput. Multi-tenant needs eviction heuristics and admission control. Our approach is three levers: hard fencing (dedicated), soft fencing (reserved concurrency + weight), and runtime QoS (burst tokens, preemptible slots).
[02:05] Jin Park: When you say cache warm per tenant for dedicated, how long to build the KV for a model with long contexts? Warm up during a session is what worries us.
[02:18] Priya: For long-context models we do progressive prefetch: on session start we prime the KV with recent embeddings and the opening tokens, then we continue prefetching as tokens are generated. Dedicated gives you the fastest priming time because cache never evicts for other tenants. In multi-tenant, you'd schedule prefetching with priority hints to reduce cold hit penalties.
[02:42] Tom: Any numbers for cold vs warm tail latency?
[02:46] Liam: Ballpark from similar workloads: cold-first-token latency can be 2–3x higher if the KV isn't warm. Warmed KV path keeps token latency tight — say 30–40ms per token on our optimized kernels for that model class; cold could jump to 120–200ms for the initial chunk while KV pages are fetched and batch scheduling stabilizes. Those numbers vary with batch size and quantization.
[03:12] Sara: Quantization — we were told Int8 drops quality slightly but helps throughput; how does it affect tail latency?
[03:20] Priya: Good point. Lower precision can reduce per-token compute time and memory footprint, which helps batch more effectively and reduces queuing. However, quantized kernels sometimes have higher variance on GPU due to dequant/decompress steps, so you can see a slightly fatter tail in some microbenchmarks. We recommend model-specific evals; for many user-facing tasks q4_0 or int8 with calibration works well.
[03:47] Aisha: So is the advice to run dedicated for our payments flows, and hosted for less critical, or is there a hybrid?
[03:56] Maya: Hybrid is common: critical routes on dedicated capacity with pinned cache and reserved concurrency; less critical routes on hosted with fallbacks. We also support automatic fallback routing — if dedicated is saturated, traffic can failover to a compatible, slightly lower-capacity model in hosted with rate shaping.

[04:12] ------------------ Batching & latency SLOs ------------------
[04:15] Liam: On batching: continuous batching gives good throughput efficiency but can add head-of-line wait. For 99th percentile SLOs you often set a maximum batch latency (e.g., 5–8ms) and a max batch size. That reduces queuing for tail latency. Also we support priority queues where low-latency traffic bypasses batching for a small cost.
[04:41] Jin: Can we mark payment-critical requests to bypass batching?
[04:44] Priya: Yes, you can tag tokens or routes with priority. Cost goes up but you get deterministic latency. For your qps, a small dedicated pool with priority lanes is doable.

[04:58] ------------------ KV eviction & prefetch ------------------
[05:00] Liam: Eviction policy matters: LRU works but gets noisy with flash bursts. We implement a multi-tier eviction: hot-key pinning (lock a small working set), adaptive TTLs based on access frequency, and prefetch hints from clients. For on-prem/VPC you can enlarge the cache size and use persistent cache volumes to reduce cold-start impact.
[05:28] Tom: What's your recommendation for prefetch window sizing for sessions that go to 600 tokens?
[05:34] Priya: For 600 token sessions we prefetch the next 128 tokens in sliding windows to keep memory reasonable and avoid overfetch. You can adjust based on observed token step patterns. Prefetch agressiveness trades off memory and prefetch bandwidth.
[05:49] Aisha: Are there known noisy-neighbor attack patterns we should be concerned about? Like a tenant spinning up many short sessions to evict others' cache?
[05:58] Liam: Yes that's a real vector. We mitigate via rate limits at the tenancy level, cache residency quotas, and detection of pathological access patterns. In Dedicated those vectors are much reduced because you control the pool.

[06:12] ------------------ VPC / On-prem considerations ------------------
[06:15] Maya: On VPC/private deployments we give you the same control plane but customer traffic stays in your VPC. You get integration points for KMS/HSM, SAML SSO, and private peering. On-prem adds more ops work — we supply an operator guide and a runbook.
[06:30] Sara: For on-prem, are audit logs push or pull? We need an immutable store in our environment.
[06:36] Priya: Logs can be forwarded to your SIEM via syslog/HTTPS. We can also keep a minimal audit in the control plane but for compliance customers prefer pushing to their own immutable storage.

[06:47] ------------------ Fallbacks & Guarantees ------------------
[06:50] Liam: Important design pattern: SLA guardrail. Option A: firm reserved capacity (dedicated) with contractual SLO for throughput and p99 latency. Option B: best-effort hosted with retries and exponential backoff. Option C: hybrid with warm standby hosted pools and model downgrades.
[07:08] Tom: How do you ensure graceful degradation if dedicated pool overloads? We can't have payments stalls.
[07:14] Maya: We recommend a cascade: primary dedicated -> warm-standby dedicated in another AZ or smaller hosted variant -> token-shed or degrade response fidelity. Also we can add client-side circuit breaker logic to fail fast and queue transactions rather than blocking sync payments.
[07:30] Jin: Client-side queueing is OK but adds complexity for us. We'd prefer the server-side fallback to guarantee a bounded latency.
[07:36] Priya: For bounded latency you need reserved capacity or hard limits on concurrency. Soft fallbacks without reserved capacity can still produce spikes.

[07:45] ------------------ Real-world example & numbers ------------------
[07:48] Liam: Example: for a 10-GPU dedicated pool serving your hot route, we predict ~1.2k sustained throughput with p95 ~35–45ms token time, p99 ~85–120ms (with pinned KV). On hosted fallback to a 4-GPU equivalent model, p95 rises to ~80ms and p99 to ~220ms. That's model and kernel dependent.
[08:12] Aisha: That delta matters. If we accept occasional fallback, what's the SLA commitment?
[08:17] Maya: For dedicated we include commit and a contractual SLO. For fallback hosted we can provide best-effort and runbooks for warm standby; if you need contractual guarantees across both, you'd want multi-regional dedicated capacity.

[08:30] ------------------ Questions from Security ------------------
[08:32] Sara: A few specifics: is KMS per-tenant or shared? Do you support HSM-backed keys? And where are the encryption-at-rest keys stored for KV cache snapshots?
[08:45] Priya: We support customer-managed keys (BYOK) via KMS integrations and HSM for Private. Cache snapshots stored on encrypted volumes in the customer's VPC for private deployments; for hosted we use envelope encryption with customer keys option. We'll share concrete architecture diagrams in the security packet.
[09:02] Sara: Also need artifact proving we don't persist raw card numbers in logs.
[09:07] Maya: We can add a data flow diagram and redaction config. We'll include sample redaction regex and retention policy in the next package.

[09:15] ------------------ Tradeoffs & Recommendation ------------------
[09:18] Liam: For NovaPay given the throughput, audit needs, and p99 sensitivity — recommended approach: start pilot with a small dedicated pool for the critical payment routing (pin KV, reserve concurrency) + a warm-hosted standby in another region as fallback. Run a 2-week spike test during billing cycle end to observe tail behavior and tweak prefetch windows.
[09:42] Tom: How do we do load tests without affecting real traffic?
[09:45] Maya: We'll provide a synthetic load harness and a test plan; we can replay anonymized production traces if you want, with redaction.

[09:55] ------------------ Open discussion / misc notes ------------------
[09:56] Aisha: One more ops question — how quickly can we scale dedicated capacity if we hit sustained higher throughput?
[10:02] Priya: Autoscaling for dedicated is supported with a few minutes of buffer, but first GPU spin up and model load can take a few minutes. For strict traffic surges, pre-warming or maintaining a buffer of warm machines is recommended.
[10:15] Jin: Any suggestions on observability hooks? We need token-level tracing with sample traces 
[10:21] Liam: We provide per-token cost and latency metrics, per-route traces, and KV hit/miss metrics. We'll also expose an event stream for unusual eviction or noisy neighbor alerts.

[10:30] ------------------ Closing recap ------------------
[10:31] Maya: To recap: recommended pilot: dedicated small pool for critical route, pin KV, priority lanes for low-latency traffic, warm-hosted fallback, KMS BYOK integration for secrets, retention and redaction runbook, and a 2-week spike test.
[10:46] Aisha: Sounds right. We'll need pricing and a pilot statement-of-work.
[10:50] Maya: We'll send pricing and SOW. Also the security packet and runbook.
[10:55] Tom: Can you share the prefetch and eviction configs examples?
[10:58] Priya: Yes, we'll share sample configs and the load harness.
[11:02] Sara: Please include manifest for audit log forwarding.
[11:05] Maya: Noted. Anything else?
[11:07] Aisha: That's it, thank you.
[11:10] Maya: Great — we'll follow up with artifacts. Wrap at ~56:40.
